newsitem.title: UK: World grain stocks seen recovering from perilous lows.
newsitem.headline: World grain stocks seen recovering from perilous lows.

text.p: The International Wheat Council (IGC) raised its forecast on Friday for the 1996 world wheat harvest and said stocks should begin to recover from recent perilous lows. The London-based council, regarded by the trade as an authoritative monitor of grains supply and demand, lifted its estimate of the wheat harvest by 3.0 million tonnes from its previous estimate to 563 million.
This is up from 539 million last year. The better 1996 crops follow a period when drought ravaged Australia, North Africa and Russia.
In its latest monthly report, the IGC also saw world wheat trade at 89 million tonnes, down 4.0 million from last month's prediction and the lowest in the past 11 years.

This reflects lower import demand, mainly by China. Benchmark Chicago grains futures prices have already eased from historic highs set earlier this year -- falling below $5 per bushel from a peak at $7.50 in March -- on a prospect that some of the tension is going out of the market. The IGC said that the higher output and lower demand would help stocks recover slightly after being dangerously depleted to the lowest in 20 years, mainly because of the recent droughts. Its new estimate for 1996/97 wheat stocks is 101 million tonnes, compared with 97 million in the year just ended. But the new stock figure is still lower than at any time for 18 years.
"There will be some stock rebuilding but not to monster levels that we've seen in the 1980s," said Bill De Maria, executive assistant director of the IGC.
The sharp decline in trade was mainly due to a lower projection for Chinese purchases due to an improvement in local production, the IGC said.
The estimate of Chinese wheat imports was slashed to 9.0 million tonnes for 1996/97 from an estimated 12.7 million in the previous season.
The IGC cut its estimate for world output of coarse grains -- mainly maize (corn) -- in 1996 by 10.0 million tonnes to 866 million tonnes, mainly due a lower projection of U.S. maize.
But a crop of this size would still be a record and 69 million tonnes more than in 1995.
